Extract the coefficients of a fitted model

Source: R/model-classes.R, R/model-rf.R
spatial_fit-coef.Rd

coef() on a GWR returns the local coefficients, one row per observation and one column per term. On a Bayesian GP fit it returns the posterior summary of the global regression terms. A random forest has no coefficients, so coef() on an rf_fit always stops with an error rather than returning NULL; a forest's variable importance is in fit$info$importance (see fit_rf_model()). None of the three returns NULL (see "The coef() contract" in new_spatial_fit()).

Usage

# S3 method for class 'gwr_fit'
coef(object, se = FALSE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'bayesian_fit'
coef(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'rf_fit'
coef(object, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted gwr_fit, bayesian_fit or rf_fit.

se

GWR only. Logical; also return the standard errors and t values. Default FALSE.

...

Not used.

Value

For a GWR with se = FALSE, a data.frame of local coefficient estimates: one row per observation, one column per model term. With se = TRUE, a list of three such data.frames: estimate, se and t. An engine without an SDF component is an error.

For a Bayesian GP fit, a matrix of fixed-effect posterior summaries, as brms::fixef() returns them, on the fitted scale (per standard deviation of each predictor under standardize_predictors = TRUE), in the units of the response: where the response was handed to brms less a centre or divided by a scale, the intercept has the centre added back and every column is multiplied by the scale (see "The response's centre and scale" in fit_bayesian_spatial_model()). brms::fixef() on object$engine answers on the scale brms was given. A missing brms or a failing fixef() call is an error.

For a random forest, nothing: the call is an error.

Details

The GWR table shows where, and by how much, a predictor's relationship with the response changes across the study area: read the spread of its column, or join the table back to object$data_sf to map it. plot.spatial_fit() draws that map.

The Bayesian GP summary gives the estimate, error and credible interval of each predictor, as brms::fixef() reports them. The Gaussian-process term has already taken up the spatially structured part of the signal, so these are effects net of location (see "Spatial confounding" in fit_bayesian_spatial_model()).

GWR columns

Only the model terms are returned: the intercept and one column per predictor. The engine's SDF data slot holds more beside them (standard errors, t values, the observed response, the fitted values, the residuals, Local_R2); read object$engine$SDF for those, and ask for the standard errors and t values with se = TRUE.

A coefficient is NA at a location whose local window cannot estimate it: a predictor that does not vary among the observations that carry weight there has no slope, and the intercept is then not identified either unless the predictor is 0 there. object$info$nonfinite_coef is the mask, and fit_gwr_model() raises a warning that counts them.

If the model terms cannot be located in the SDF (an engine that names its coefficient columns differently), the whole slot is returned, with a WARN line in the log saying so (a log record, not an R warning; see spatialkit_quiet()). With se = TRUE the call stops instead. It never returns a silently short table.

GWR standard errors

With se = TRUE the local standard errors and t values come with the estimates. A standard error is \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{(C C^\top)_{jj}}\), with \(C = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W\) the weights the local regression puts on the responses and \(\hat\sigma^2\) the residual sum of squares over the fit's effective degrees of freedom: the definition GWmodel::gwr.basic() uses, computed from the QR decomposition that gave the estimate. They treat the bandwidth as known. The t values are one test per term and location, tens to thousands of them and strongly dependent, so a map of \(|t| > 2\) overstates what is significant; no p-value, adjusted or not, is returned. An adjustment for the number of tests can use the t values here, the effective number of parameters object$info$enp and the residual degrees of freedom object$info$edf. When observations share a location the standard errors are too small as well (see "Observations that share a location" in fit_gwr_model()).

Bayesian GP standardised predictors

The summaries are on the scale the model was fitted on. A fit made with standardize_predictors = TRUE was fitted on centred and scaled numeric predictors, so each slope is the change in the linear predictor per standard deviation of its predictor and the intercept is its value at the predictor means, not the raw-unit numbers stats::lm() reports on the same formula. The returned matrix does not say so; print() on the fit does, and the centre and scale of each predictor are in object$info$predictor_scaling. To put a slope back in raw units divide its Estimate, Est.Error and interval bounds by that predictor's scale. The intercept's Estimate follows by linearity (subtract each raw-unit slope times its predictor's center), but its Est.Error and interval depend on the posterior covariance of the coefficients: transform the draws from brms::as_draws_df(object$engine) for those, or refit without standardising.

See also

Other fit methods: plot.spatial_fit(), print.spatial_fit(), spatial_fit-fitted, spatial_fit-predict, spatial_fit-residuals, summary.spatial_fit()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
n <- 80
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
             a = rnorm(n)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
# The slope on a rises from west to east.
east <- (st_coordinates(pts)[, 1] - 5e5) / 1000
pts$z <- 10 + (1 + 2 * east) * pts$a + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
gw <- fit_gwr_model(pts, "z", "a", bandwidth = 30)
str(coef(gw, se = TRUE))
#> List of 3
#>  $ estimate:'data.frame':	80 obs. of  2 variables:
#>   ..$ Intercept: num [1:80] 10.09 9.9 10.06 10.21 9.99 ...
#>   ..$ a        : num [1:80] 1.53 1.62 2.17 2.74 1.45 ...
#>  $ se      :'data.frame':	80 obs. of  2 variables:
#>   ..$ Intercept: num [1:80] 0.0757 0.0736 0.079 0.0786 0.0734 ...
#>   ..$ a        : num [1:80] 0.0792 0.0852 0.0802 0.0845 0.0875 ...
#>  $ t       :'data.frame':	80 obs. of  2 variables:
#>   ..$ Intercept: num [1:80] 133 135 127 130 136 ...
#>   ..$ a        : num [1:80] 19.3 19 27 32.4 16.6 ...
summary(coef(gw)$a)     # the local slopes span the west-east change
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.325   1.596   1.967   2.075   2.603   2.780
